 Children's Hospital LA joins warning on holiday toy risks 
 Federal regulators also have cautioned against a social-media trend encouraging children to heat squishy toys. 
 By City News Service • 
 Published 3 hours ago • 
 Updated 3 hours ago 
 BOOKMARKER 
 Getty 
 Los Angeles-area families hunting for holiday gifts were urged Tuesday to look beyond the newest toys' packaging and price tags, with a consumer report warning of potential hazards involving squishy toys, artificial intelligence chatbots, counterfeits and online purchases from unfamiliar sellers. 
 CALPIRG Education Fund's annual "Trouble in Toyland'' report highlighted five categories of toys that it said could pose particular safety concerns this holiday season. The report was released with input from Children's Hospital Los Angeles, where an injury-prevention official warned that changes in the toy marketplace require parents and gift-givers to closely consider age recommendations and safety information.

 "The toy market is evolving rapidly, in frightening ways,'' CALPIRG Education Fund State Director Jenn Engstrom said in a statement. "Four out of five of these problems didn't represent a significant threat 10 years ago.''
 One concern involves squishy and squeezy fidget toys, some of which contain water beads that can expand inside a child's body if swallowed. The Consumer Product Safety Commission has warned that counterfeit squishy toys may fail federal standards for water beads, small parts, lead, phthalates and other hazardous substances. 
 Federal regulators also have cautioned against a social-media trend encouraging children to heat squishy toys. The toys can burst when heated, releasing hot material that may cause serious burns, according to the CPSC.
 The report also cited pull-string activity and teething toys for toddlers and infants. It said nearly a half-million of those toys were recalled or targeted in government warnings in the past year because of choking and other hazards. 
 Researchers tested seven AI-powered toys designed to converse with children and found that some could be prompted to discuss sexual topics or give information about finding potentially dangerous household objects, according to the report.

 "Just a few years ago, AI toys didn't even exist,'' R.J. Cross, Our Online Life campaign director for U.S. PIRG Education Fund and a co-author of the report, said in a statement. "Now, once again, our testing has uncovered
poorly designed chatbot toys with glitchy guardrails that deteriorate the longer you talk to them.'' 
 Cross said the toys use chatbots "meant for adults'' and warned that talking companion toys are not appropriate for young children.   
 The report also urged families to be cautious when buying toys online from unfamiliar sellers, particularly newer international marketplaces, where products may not meet U.S. safety requirements. 
 It also warned that recalled and counterfeit toys remain widely available despite being illegal to sell. 
 From January through July, the CPSC issued more than 900 notices of violation involving toy shipments, according to the report. CALPIRG said individual shipments often contain hundreds or thousands of the same item, and more than one-quarter of the shipments were not seized at the border. 
 The report said toy-related emergency room injuries have increased every year since 2020, with half involving children 4 and younger. 
 "As holiday shopping season gets underway, it's important for parents and gift-givers to consider the age-appropriateness and safety ramifications involved before purchasing toys for kids,'' Helen Arbogast, manager of injury prevention at Children's Hospital Los Angeles, said in a statement. "With toy-related injuries on the rise and an evolution in the types of toys being marketed to children, families must read the fine print and be aware of the red flags to look out for to avoid preventable toy-related injuries.'' 
 CALPIRG advised shoppers to check toys for recalls, buy from reputable sellers, follow age recommendations and avoid products with missing manufacturer information, safety warnings or tracking labels.
